philadelphia.intro: Philadelphia's oldest tree came from London in 1785. It is the ginkgo at Bartram's Garden, the oldest known in North America, and a few steps from it a yellowwood over 200 years old is still blooming after lightning left it hollow and wired together. Across the city, the sidewalk on Hobson Street bends round a scholar tree, a sycamore outside Washington Square outlived the famous Moon Tree, and two old cemeteries keep state champions. Three more trees stand at Morris Arboretum, which charges admission. The other six are free.
philadelphia.meta_description: Nine remarkable trees in Philadelphia, from America's oldest ginkgo at Bartram's Garden to a Hobson Street tree the sidewalk bends around.
philadelphia.question_meta: Bartram's Ginkgo, planted 1785, roughly 240 years old, is Philadelphia's oldest tree and America's oldest ginkgo, one of nine mapped here.
philadelphia.question_answer: The oldest tree in Philadelphia is Bartram's Ginkgo, growing east of the Bartram Barn at Bartram's Garden in Southwest Philadelphia, believed to be around 240 years old. It grew from a sapling William Hamilton shipped from London in 1785 and gave to his friend William Bartram, and it is thought to be the oldest ginkgo in North America. In the same garden, an American yellowwood beside the Bartram House is over 200 years old by the garden's account, though no source gives its planting year. Both are free to see.
philadelphia.question_context:
The ginkgo's date rests on a specific claim. In 1785 William Hamilton of The Woodlands shipped three ginkgo saplings from London, the first of their kind to reach North America. He kept two at his estate and gave the third to William Bartram, whose garden on the Schuylkill is the oldest surviving botanic garden on the continent. Hamilton's two were cut down in the 1980s, leaving Bartram's the sole survivor.

Its nearest rival for age stands a few steps away. The yellowwood in the Kitchen Garden has reigned there for more than 200 years, the garden says, probably from a plant the explorer André Michaux gathered in Tennessee, and it survived a 2010 storm that left it hollow and wired together.

Hamilton's old estate is now The Woodlands cemetery, where a champion Caucasian zelkova grows by his mansion. Laurel Hill Cemetery keeps a champion cut-leaf linden, a Hobson Street scholar tree had a neighbourhood planned around it, and a big sycamore stands on the 6th Street side of Washington Square. Those six are free. At Morris Arboretum, which charges admission, stand a Bender oak, a katsura and a weeping hemlock from the 1876 Centennial Exposition.

faq_add.q: Which old trees can I see for free in Philadelphia?
faq_add.a: Six of the nine on this page are free. Bartram's Ginkgo and the Bartram Yellowwood stand in Bartram's Garden, open free every day from dawn to dusk. The champion zelkova is at The Woodlands cemetery and the cut-leaf linden at Laurel Hill Cemetery, both free during gate hours. The Hobson Street scholar tree and the Washington Square sycamore are on public sidewalks, there at any hour.

faq_add.q: Is there a remarkable tree in Center City?
faq_add.a: Yes. On the 6th Street sidewalk just outside the wall of Washington Square stands a sycamore that Philadelphia Parks & Recreation calls likely the largest in Center City. It is free and open at all hours, a short walk from the Walnut-Locust stations. The square's Moon Tree, a sycamore planted in 1975, has died; only its plaque remains.

faq_add.q: Why does the sidewalk on Hobson Street curve?
faq_add.a: To go round a scholar tree. Philadelphia Parks & Recreation says the tree survived several development projects, the neighbourhood was planned around it, and the sidewalk bends out round its base, taking a parking space. It stands opposite Buist Park in Elmwood.

faq_replace.Is it free to visit?: Bartram's Garden is. It is a city-owned public garden and National Historic Landmark, free and open every day, dawn to dusk. So are The Woodlands and Laurel Hill cemeteries during their gate hours, and the Hobson Street and Washington Square trees on public sidewalks. Morris Arboretum, where three of the nine trees on this page stand, charges general admission.

media-pennsylvania.intro: Tyler Arboretum, outside Media in Delaware County, still keeps 21 plants that the Painter brothers set out between the 1840s and the 1860s. Three of them are here. A giant sequoia counted the largest in Pennsylvania lost its top in 1895 and grew several spires in its place. A ginkgo stands behind Lachford Hall. And the state's champion Cedar of Lebanon is in decline, by the arboretum's own account. Tyler charges admission, and from Center City Philadelphia it is well over half an hour by public transport, nearer an hour or more.
media-pennsylvania.meta_description: Three Painter-era trees at Tyler Arboretum near Media, PA: Pennsylvania's largest giant sequoia, a ginkgo and a champion Cedar of Lebanon.
media-pennsylvania.question_meta: Tyler Arboretum's giant sequoia, planted around 1856 by one account, is counted Pennsylvania's largest. Three Painter-era trees are mapped here.
media-pennsylvania.question_answer: The best-known old tree near Media is the giant sequoia at Tyler Arboretum, counted the largest in Pennsylvania by the arboretum and Wikipedia and the state champion since 1950. The Painter brothers planted it around 1856, by one account, inside a planting window the arboretum gives as the 1840s to the 1860s, so it is roughly 170 years old. In 2006 it measured 29 metres tall and 3.93 metres round.
media-pennsylvania.question_context:
Tyler Arboretum keeps what survives of the trees two brothers, the Painters, planted on this ground in the middle of the nineteenth century. Of what they put in, 21 plants of 19 species survive, and the arboretum keeps them as its legacy collection, fenced to protect the roots and marked with blue tags.

The giant sequoia is the famous one. Its central leader was cut off in 1895, which is why it carries several spires, and it is treated every year against fungal disease and fitted with lightning protection. It grows above Painter Road. The ginkgo, behind Lachford Hall, has no published measurements; in November it turns yellow. The Cedar of Lebanon is listed as Pennsylvania's state champion by the Scott Arboretum and Wikipedia, and the arboretum says it is in decline. Its exact spot is not published, so ask at the entrance.

No planting year is recorded for the ginkgo or the cedar, so their ages come from the Painters' window, about 160 to 185 years. Tyler charges admission. The nearest rail is Media station on the Media/Wawa line, several kilometres off, then a taxi or local bus; allow an hour or more from Center City Philadelphia.

faq.q: Can you get to Tyler Arboretum by public transport?
faq.a: Not directly. No SEPTA stop serves the gate. Take the Media/Wawa line to Media station, several kilometres away, then a taxi or local bus. From Center City Philadelphia that is well over half an hour, nearer an hour or more door to door.

No. Adults pay $18, seniors $15 and ages 3 to 17 $10; under 3 is free. It is open daily, 9 am to 6 pm from April to October and 9 am to 4 pm from November to March, and closed on Thanksgiving and 24 and 25 December.

faq.q: Where is the giant sequoia at Tyler Arboretum?
faq.a: Above Painter Road. Look for several spires instead of one point, the result of its top being cut off in 1895, and for the fence, blue Painter legacy tag and lightning rod.
